newsitem.title: USA: ABA official sees slower U.S. economy next year.
newsitem.headline: ABA official sees slower U.S. economy next year.

text.p: Joel Naroff, chairman of the American Bankers Association Economic Advisory Committee, said Thursday it was expected that the economy would slow next year but it was unlikely it would tumble into recession.

He told a briefing for reporters following a conference call with the banks' advisory committee that economic growth might increase by one to 1-1/2 percent next year but there was even the possibility of one negative quarter during that period.
"We don't see a recession but there is the possibility of two pretty soft quarters next year," he said.
Naroff said that as the economy weakens, the bank economists take the view that interest rates may lower, although he gave no specific indication of by how much or when that would occur.
The ABA will unveil its official economic outlook on January 29.
Turning to the election that gave President Clinton a second term and left the Republican party in charge of Congress, Naroff said this increased the possibility of a budget deal.

At the same time, he said that banks are being more conservative in consumer loans and may be in the early stages of examining industries that may be hurt by an economic slowdown in reviewing lending policy.

Turning to the Federal Reserve, he said that the central bank is probably being cautious about moving to a more neutral stance because it had been surprised by the very strong second quarter and wanted to make sure that this might not happen again.
But he said on balance it appeared that the economy was beginning to slow and that 1997 would be less vigorous than in the recent period.
